content.title: Measles (Rubeola) | Division of Public Health
content.text: Frequently Asked Questions Tab/Accordion Items Measles exposure happens if:You share indoor space with someone who has measles and can spread it, orYou go into an indoor space within two hours after a person with measles leaves.People with measles can spread it to others from four days before through four days after the rash appears.NC Exposure Locations This guidance is for public places like stores, restaurants, community centers and recreation facilities. There are separate resources for local health departments and health care providers and for child care, schools and universities.If a person with measles spent time at your location, other people may have been exposed.Your local health department will reach out and work with you to find out who was exposed. Please be prepared to help with this process. You may be asked for contact details for staff, customers and visitors at your location during the exposure period.Local and state public health teams notify people of their exposure by phone, text or in-person visit. These teams share what to do if you were exposed to measles. The information you share helps guide these important notifications.If confirmed as an exposure location, your location will be added to the NC Exposure Locations page.A staff member with measles exposure may be asked to show their local health department records of the MMR vaccine or past illness.People without proof of immunity may need to stay home and avoid others for 21 days after they were last exposed. Your local health department will help with this guidance. They can also help by giving work notes for people who are told to stay home and avoid others. These notes can be shared with employers.How you can prepareEnsure staff understand that they may be asked to provide their vaccine records to their local health department.Download/share fact sheets and more with your staff and educate them about measles, including symptoms and how it spreads.Maintain routine cleaning and disinfection of your business. Measles is not likely to be transmitted by touching surfaces.Restaurants should follow all safe food handling, preparation, cooking and cleaning requirements of the NC Food Code. Measles is not spread through food or drinks. Yes, but getting measles if you've been vaccinated is rare. If this happens, symptoms are usually milder.One dose of MMR vaccine is about 93% effective at preventing measles. Two doses are about 97% effective. Vitamin A cannot prevent measles. The MMR vaccine is the best way to protect against measles. Only take vitamin A when directed by a health care provider. Providers may give vitamin A to some people diagnosed with measles as part of their care plan.About Vitamin AMost people get enough vitamin A in their diet through foods like:Vegetables like carrots, bell peppers and broccoliFish and chickenYogurtYou can take too much vitamin A, known as toxicity, since it builds up in the body over time. In pregnancy, vitamin A toxicity can cause birth defects. Symptoms of vitamin A toxicityDizzinessBlurred visionNausea and vomitingHeadache Measles typically starts with cough, runny nose, and red eyes. It often leads to a rash and fever above 101 degrees Fahrenheit. If you think you have measles, get medical care.Don't delay: Symptoms can get worse over time, leading to complications and even death.Seek emergency medical care immediately if you have any of these signs:A hard time breathing or breathing faster than normalSigns of severe dehydration (dry nose and mouth, urinating less than usual)Confusion, decreased alertness, or severe weaknessFor young children:A blue color around the mouthCrying without making tearsUnusually low energySevere loss of appetiteIn the event of an emergency, call 911.Alert your care team to protect othersHave someone call the emergency room or your provider. Let them know a person with measles is coming in so they can prepare and take steps to protect you and others.
